Dans la culture latino-américaine, il es: In Latin American culture, it is normal for older people to age alongside their children under the same roof. When older people are more independent, it is common for them to live a few streets away from their families, to make sure that, whatever happens, there is always someone to help them.
Cela devient une préoccupation supplémen: This becomes an added concern when migration is involved. Many parents end up immigrating to Quebec once their children have found a certain stability in the province, especially if the conditions that prompted the migration persist in the country of origin.
Ce fut le cas avec les groupes de migran: This was the case with the Latin American migrant groups of the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s, which included many parents and grandparents from Chile, Argentina, Central America, Colombia and, more recently, Mexico, Peru and Venezuela.
Aujourd’hui, il est de plus en plus fréq: Today, it is increasingly common at gatherings, parties and picnics for Latino families to seek out other families who have their parents in Quebec, in order to socialize. For many, caring for parents requires a strategy and planning similar to what is needed for the youngest children.
En effet, les personnes âgées immigrées: Indeed, older immigrants of Latin American origin don’t necessarily find it easy to integrate into Quebec society, despite the abundance of services for seniors in Quebec. One barrier generally keeps them from going out, socializing and maintaining some autonomy, even though they are resourceful: language.
Il n’existe pas de données précises sur: There is no precise data on the number of older people of Latin American origin living in Quebec. According to <l1>a report</l1> presented last March at the annual meeting of the Groupe d’expertise pour le développement de cités interculturelles au Québec, in 2016, about 44% of seniors living in Montréal were born outside Canada.
Selon les statistiques du gouvernement f: According to federal government statistics, 96% of immigrants aged 65 and over arrived in Canada before 2006.

Cette grand-mère aux cheveux gris et au: This grey-haired grandmother with a mischievous gaze worked for 40 years as a secretary in Venezuela and studied law when she was already older. The political, economic and social situation in that South American country and the constant pleas of her daughter Laura led her to settle permanently in Quebec.
Doris est arrivée le 31 juillet 2021 à H: Doris arrived on July 31, 2021, in Hochelaga, at the home of Laura, her husband and her son. She came through the Government of Canada’s Parents and Grandparents Program. “I didn’t want to come, but I started thinking about what I would do alone in Venezuela,” she recalls. “If something happened to me, nobody would find me for several days, by which time I’d already be rotten,” adds the soft-spoken, cheerful woman, laughing.
Alors âgée de 80 ans, elle décide de pre: At 80, she decided to take French classes. She learned to make the round trip by public transit, and did so for a few months, to attend the classes, but they were not suited to her level.
Sa fille Laura est son principal soutien: Her daughter Laura is her main support. She looked for other ways for her mother to keep learning French. A French course for people who can’t read or write was suggested, but Laura felt it would not suit Doris’s needs either.
Un portrait de Laura et Doris. Photo: Pa: A portrait of Laura and Doris. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Elles ont fini par trouver un cours à te: They eventually found a part-time course that was a little less demanding. Even though the family recently moved to Anjou, Doris still attends a school near Hochelaga.
« Ici, le seul contact que j’ai en dehor: “Here, the only contact I have outside the house is with my classmates. The classes are very hard for me and, on top of that, most of my classmates are young. I always ask the boy behind me to tell me what the teacher said,” she says, laughing.
Bien que Doris ait fait une chute une fo: Although Doris once fell and hurt herself during an ice storm, she is always ready to go out and live her life. “I’ve always been independent and I use public transit. What stops me is that I don’t speak French. If I go out, I can’t talk to anyone, unless of course I meet someone who speaks Spanish,” she laments. She also attends the church Notre-Dame-de-Guadalupe (Latin American Mission), on rue de Bordeaux in Montréal, but she hesitates to take part in the activities held there every Sunday. So far, the family has not found suitable Spanish-language services near home.
Bien que la présence de sa mère au Québe: Although her mother’s presence in Quebec gives Laura some peace of mind, a doubt creeps into her thoughts from time to time. “There are times when I wonder if bringing her here was really the best decision. When you’re older, you’re not always ready to leave your country, to leave your things, your friends… I think maybe it would be better for her to go back to Venezuela, but then I tell myself she would be alone, that anything could happen to her, and at that point, the doubt disappears.”
Pour Laura, il est essentiel qu’il y ait: For Laura, it is essential that there be places for these seniors who don’t speak French to meet. “Ideally there would be more places where they could talk, play, knit, go on guided walks, but in Spanish. As much as they need to integrate into Quebec, they also need to socialize in their own language, because the pace of learning isn’t the same. We shouldn’t demand of older people what we demand of ourselves. They are at a different stage of life,” she points out.
Ces lieux de rencontre sont généralement: These meeting places are generally offered by community centres and immigrant aid organizations. One of these centres, well known to Montréal’s Latin American community, is the Centre d’aide aux familles latino-américaines (CAFLA). It offers community support services to immigrants, with particular attention to early childhood and youth. It also has a listening and psychological support service in Spanish for the whole family, including older people.
Cecilia Escamilla, directrice du CAFLA,: Cecilia Escamilla, director of CAFLA, would like to set up a program exclusively for older people of Latin American origin, but she knows it would take more than goodwill. The resources Quebec provides for this type of program are not sufficient, she believes.
« Chaque année, le ministère responsable: “Every year, the ministry responsible for seniors can allocate around $25,000 to a CAFLA project, but with that amount, we can’t even pay a full-time human resources person. When there were calls for proposals for projects, we took part in order to plan activities for Latino seniors, to give them information, to help them translate documents, but it’s not possible with so few resources,” she laments.
Le CAFLA, qui célèbre cette année son 20: CAFLA, which is celebrating its 20<sup>th</sup> anniversary this year, has tried over the years to set up programs for older people, but for now offers only psychological support. “We developed several projects for our seniors, but our space is currently on the second floor, and we can’t welcome them for activities, which is why we redirect them to other organizations,” she says.
Pour Cecilia, le besoin de services en e: For Cecilia, the need for Spanish-language services has grown as the first groups of immigrants have aged. “Many older people arrived 15 or 20 years ago with their children to take care of their grandchildren. They weren’t fully integrated into life in Quebec. They didn’t take francization classes, didn’t socialize with people their own age. Their grandchildren grew up and left home, but the grandparents stayed. Church on Sunday is practically their only outing,” she explains.
Il y a eu des cas de grands-parents aban: There have been cases of grandparents who were abandoned, assaulted by their own children and even financially exploited, she says. The money they received from social assistance or pensions was taken from them by their children. “We’ve had older people crying in front of our offices because they didn’t know what to do. Some were abandoned because their children remarried and moved to another province, or because the new spouse doesn’t accept the grandparent in the home,” she laments.
Selon elle, il faut aussi qu’il y ait un: In her view, there also needs to be a paradigm shift within Latin American culture, to allow older people to remain as independent as possible.
« Nous agissons de façon à ce que nos pa: “We act in ways that have our parents going out to eat with us, going to our parties, having us take them to church. We treat them like children, we infantilize them, we diminish them instead of fostering their autonomy. And all of this because we think they are incapable, when in fact an older person has already come a long way and can do more than we can,” she warns.

He says he is happy since arriving in Montréal more than a year ago, but Lourdes and her partner have the impression that he is not. “We think he might even be suffering from some kind of depression, because sometimes we find him in front of the television, but it’s turned off,” says Lourdes. She is looking for resources to help her father-in-law integrate better into Quebec society.
Une organisation propose aux personnes â: One organization offers seniors activities in French near their home. Pedro was offered the chance to attend some of them so he could socialize. He chose not to go.
« Il fait beaucoup d’efforts pour appren: “He makes a lot of effort to learn French, but he’s afraid to speak. It’s been very hard for him and he despairs, but he keeps trying. It’s a very difficult situation.”
Jorge Huenufil est lui aussi un beau-pèr: Jorge Huenufil is also a father-in-law who recently arrived in Quebec. Originally from Chile, he looks to be in great shape. He worked for more than 45 years at one of the country’s largest newspaper publishing houses as operations director. According to him, the last years before he emigrated took a toll on his nervous system, with consequences for his physical health. Like Doris, he is currently taking francization classes.
Jorge Huenufil vit à La Prairie avec son: Jorge Huenufil lives in La Prairie with his son and daughter-in-law. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
Venir au Canada était le dernier choix d: Coming to Canada was Jorge’s last choice: after his five children emigrated and his wife died, the 76-year-old decided it was best to spend the following years with Claudio, one of his sons, and his wife Mervic, who live in La Prairie.
Arrivé au Québec en juin 2022, il a dépo: He arrived in Quebec in June 2022 and filed a refugee claim. He has not yet had a hearing, but he has a work permit.
Pour l’instant, comme travailler n’est p: For now, since working is not in his plans, he studies French full time. He goes to school, located in the city of Sainte-Catherine, and comes back by bus. He is also studying online to become a trader.
Jorge est grand, mince et jovial. Il nou: Jorge is tall, slim and jovial. He assures us that he is in good spirits and is grateful to live here, although one senses that a certain modesty keeps him from revealing all the difficulties he has to deal with. “I like the way of life in Canada and the order. I’ve always been like that. Once I’ve decided something, I do everything I can to make it positive. It’s a state of mind,” he says, with firmness in his voice and on his face.
Mais comme pour Doris, l’apprentissage d: But as with Doris, learning French is hard for him. “It’s very heavy. I’m not 20, 30 or 40 years old, so I often have to translate what I want to say. The best thing is to be able to think in the language right away, but that’s very difficult for me.”
Il se dit reconnaissant de la manière do: He says he is grateful for the way the country treats immigrants. “I know the goal is for everyone to be productive, and that’s why I plan to keep studying. What I want is to make the most of it.”

Doris et Jorge n’ont pas d’espace pour s: Doris and Jorge have no place to socialize near home, but in the heart of Rosemont, Latino seniors have a place where they can socialize in Spanish, connect with seniors from other cultures and even move their bodies.
Le Centre d’orientation paralégale et so: The Centre d’orientation paralégale et sociale pour immigrants (COPSI) has existed for 41 years and was founded by Chilean immigrants in the 1980s. Their goal? To offer services in Spanish to their community and to other Latin American groups.
Cet organisme est d’ailleurs devenu inco: The organization has in fact become indispensable in Montréal. “People from everywhere call us for information in Spanish and, since we’re a point of reference, other organizations ask us for help,” says Jessica Fierro of COPSI. “Even the police have asked us to help older people who only spoke Spanish,” she adds.
Carmen González et Jessica Fierro sont r: Carmen González and Jessica Fierro run COPSI and the Le Chemin du Passé program for Latino seniors. Photo: Courtesy of COPSI
Depuis 1995, le COPSI offre – par interm: Since 1995, COPSI has offered, on and off, Spanish-language services for older people. “We’ve always had in mind the need to break isolation and prevent elder abuse,” says Carmen González, the organization’s director.
Les activités se déroulent au sous-sol d: The activities take place in the basement of Saint-Édouard church and include a kind of chair yoga, Zumba, crafts and even talks. Le Chemin du Passé also offers outings, walks and hikes, organized thanks to a grant from Quebec’s Ministry of Health.
Au COPSI, les personnes âgées ont aussi: At COPSI, seniors also have access to food baskets, with menus adapted to their needs, including plenty of vegetables. The food bank asks for an annual membership fee of $10.
Les activités de COPSI impliquent réguli: COPSI’s activities regularly involve up to 100 seniors. Photo: Courtesy of COPSI
Actuellement, 200 personnes sont inscrit: Currently, 200 people are registered in Le Chemin du Passé. The activities take place mainly in Spanish, but the space has become a cultural meeting point for older people of all origins. It allows them to reinforce what they learn in the French and Spanish classes that the organization also offers.
En ce moment, l’organisme attend les ser: Right now, the organization is waiting for the services of a Spanish-speaking priest so it can offer a Mass in Spanish, knowing that the church and its activities are one of the few things older Latinos attend on a regular basis.
Un autre aspect important du COPSI est q: Another important aspect of COPSI is that it benefits from the help of the seniors themselves, who volunteer for the activities, which not only keeps them busy and active but also gives them the feeling of being very useful.
COPSI offers outings to its members. In September, the seniors went apple picking in a field outside Montréal. Photo: Courtesy of COPSI

Le COPSI a mis en place un programme app: COPSI has set up a program called Le Chemin du Passé, which offers activities exclusively for seniors. The program, whose Spanish name is “El Camino de Antaño,” “represents the journey of our elders, their life experiences and how to use that experience to move toward the future,” sums up Ms Fierro, the program coordinator.
« Beaucoup d’entre eux mettent des vêtem: “Many of them put on special clothes to come to the activities. They appreciate that we give them life, joy. One time, we organized an activity in a park for the whole family, and it was the grandmothers who ended up hitting the piñata. They thanked us for it,” says Ms Fierro.
Étant donné le nombre élevé de personnes: Given the high number of people taking part in the activities, there is a need to expand the space where these volunteers currently work, since the people who come to COPSI aren't only residents of Rosemont and the surrounding area. “They also come from Laval and the South Shore, because we know there aren't many services of this kind in Montréal and its suburbs,” adds M<sup>s</sup> González.
